TITLE: Investigating KL-Regularized Reward Maximization for Diffusion Models with Intractable Marginal Likelihoods
PROPOSAL: We propose a set of experiments investigating the efficacy of KL-regularized reward maximization for fine-tuning pre-trained diffusion models on text-to-image, document layout, and molecule generation tasks. Specifically, we compare the performance of KL-regularized Proximal Policy Optimization (KL-PPO) withReward Augmented Maximum Likelihood (RAML) objective (as an inexact KL surrogate) on the three tasks with a baseline approach that simply replaces KL term with 0.
CONTROLS: We compare to a baseline approach (i.e. ignoring KL regularization) and provide ablations over the choice of the inexact KL surrogate.
COST: We estimate this set of experiments to take around 20,000 GPU-hours (assuming ~10 experiments, each with 2,000 GPU-hours).
PREDICTION: We expect that KL-PPO will outperform the baseline and RAML on the three tasks, and that the inexact KL surrogate used in RAML may not capture the full complexity of the marginal KL divergence. However, this method may struggle with the subpar results due to the initial value function bias problem.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Exploring the Impact of Initial Value Function Bias on KL-Regularized Reward Maximization
PROPOSAL: To address the initial value function bias problem in KL-regularized reward maximization for diffusion models, we propose an experiment that investigates the impact of this bias on the performance of KL-PPO. Specifically, we implement a learned reverse process initialization scheme that adjusts the initial noise distribution based on the reward signal, and compare its performance with standard KL-PPO on the text-to-image, document layout, and molecule generation tasks.
CONTROLS: We compare this approach with standard KL-PPO and provide ablations over the choice of the initialization scheme.
COST: Estimated additional 5,000 GPU-hours (using 1,000 GPU-hours per experiment, with 5 experiments in total).
PREDICTION: We expect that the learned reverse process initialization scheme will improve the performance of KL-PPO by reducing the initial value function bias, but may require careful tuning of the initialization scheme to avoid overfitting to the reward signal.

TITLE: A Study on the Use of Best-of-N Sampling for Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We investigate the efficacy of Best-of-N sampling for fine-tuning pre-trained diffusion models on text-to-image, document layout, and molecule generation tasks. We compare the performance of Best-of-N sampling with KL-PPO and RAML on these tasks, and explore the choice of N (number of sampled trajectories to select from). Additionally, we analyze the relationship between Best-of-N sampling and KL-regularized reward maximization and, theoretically, we relate Best-of-N to policy gradient methods for this special case of diffusion models where the marginal likelihoods are easy to compute.
CONTROLS: We compare to KL-PPO, RAML, and provide ablations over the choice of N.
COST: Estimated 5,000 GPU-hours (assuming 2,000 GPU-hours per experiment, with 2.5 experiments in total).
PREDICTION: We expect that Best-of-N sampling will be effective in fine-tuning pre-trained diffusion models, but its performance may be sensitive to the choice of N.

TITLE: A Study on the Use of Best-of-N Sampling for Fine-Tuning Diffusion Models
PROPOSAL: We revise our previous proposal by adding a theoretical component that provides a deeper understanding of the relationship between Best-of-N sampling and policy gradient methods for diffusion models. Specifically, we theoretically relate the Best-of-N sampling objective to KL-regularized reward maximization and provide a proof that shows that in the limit of N going to infinity, Best-of-N sampling converges to KL-PPO.
CONTROLS: We keep the same controls as before, comparing to KL-PPO, RAML, and providing ablations over the choice of N.
COST: The compute cost remains the same, 5,000 GPU-hours.
PREDICTION: We expect that our theoretical results will provide a solid foundation for understanding the relationship between Best-of-N sampling and policy gradient methods for diffusion models, and that our theoretical bounds will show that Best-of-N sampling converges to KL-PPO in the limit of N going to infinity.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Learning to Utilize External Context in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
PROPOSAL: We will experiment with a novel training objective that encourages the model to attend to the external context (retrieved documents) equally or more than its internal knowledge, by incorporating a gradient-based imitation learning approach using a pre-trained external context utilization model. Specifically, we will leverage a model pre-trained to predict the likelihood of a generated token being supported by the external context, to guide our IM model to produce responses that rely more heavily on the retrieved context.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach to the existing ReDeEP method, and a baseline model trained with standard cross-entropy objectives. We will also perform an ablation study to assess the importance of the imitation learning component and the external context utilization model.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our proposed approach has the potential to improve the factual reliability of retrieval-augmented generation outputs, while also providing a more interpretable signal for hallucination detection. However, it may suffer from the need for additional pre-trained models and a more complex training pipeline, which could be computationally expensive.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Measuring External Context Utilization through Neural Attention Patterns
PROPOSAL: We will investigate whether neural attention patterns in multi-modal transformer architectures can serve as a signal for external context utilization. Specifically, we will use tools from information theory to analyze the mutual information between the model's attention weights and the relevant context tokens in the retrieved documents. This approach aims to capture the degree to which the model's attention mechanism is modulated by the external context.
CONTROLS: We will compare our approach to the existing ReDeEP method, which relies on attention weights from specific heads, and a baseline model with a uniform attention distribution.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our proposed approach may provide a more comprehensive understanding of how the model's attention mechanism interacts with the external context, but it may be computationally intensive and require careful tuning of hyperparameters to yield meaningful results.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Learning to Utilize External Context in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
REVISED PROPOSAL: We will modify our previous approach to incorporate a more explicit modeling of the interaction between the external context and the internal knowledge. Specifically, we will stack our original model with a modulator component that takes the attention weights over the external context and uses them to scale the output of the original model, thus encouraging the model to adapt its output based on the relevance of the context.
CONTROLS: We will compare our revised approach to the original version and the baseline model, while also performing an ablation study to assess the contribution of the modulator component.
COST: 300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our revised approach may lead to more nuanced and accurate results, but it may also introduce additional complexity and require careful tuning of hyperparameters.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Grounded Response Evaluation for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
PROPOSAL: We will develop a new evaluation metric for retrieval-augmented generation outputs, which assesses their factual reliability by comparing them to the relevant context tokens in the retrieved documents. The metric will be based on a combination of exact token matching and semantic relatedness measures.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed metric to existing metrics such as ROUGE and BLEU, as well as to human judgments of factual accuracy.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our proposed metric may provide a more effective evaluation of retrieval-augmented generation outputs, while also offering a more interpretable signal for hallucination detection. However, it may require careful tuning of parameters and may not be easily applicable to all types of generation tasks.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Understanding Hallucinations through Counterfactual Analysis
PROPOSAL: We will apply counterfactual analysis to retrieval-augmented generation outputs, where we will generate responses to the same input prompt both with and without access to the external context. This will allow us to identify which parts of the response are unique to the external context, and which parts are hallucinations.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results to existing methods for identifying hallucinations, and also perform an analysis of the types of hallucinations that occur in different contexts.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our proposed approach may provide valuable insights into the nature of hallucinations in retrieval-augmented generation, but it may require significant computational resources and may be challenging to interpret the results due to the complexity of the counterfactual analysis.

TITLE: Identifying Internal Knowledge Over-Reliance through Causal Intervention
PROPOSAL: We will use causal inference techniques to identify which internal model components are contributing to the generation of responses that are not supported by the external context. Specifically, we will perform "interventions" on the internal model variables to estimate the causal impact of these components on the response generation process.
CONTROLS: We will compare our results to existing methods for diagnosing internal knowledge over-reliance, and also perform an analysis of the robustness of our causal estimates to different model architectures and external context sources.
COST: 600 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our proposed approach may provide valuable insights into the internal knowledge dynamics that lead to hallucinations, but it may require careful calibration of the causal inference methodology and may be sensitive to the choice of intervention points.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Understanding Hallucinations through Counterfactual Analysis
REVISED PROPOSAL: We will modify our previous counterfactual analysis approach to incorporate a more sophisticated evaluation of the responses generated with and without access to the external context. Specifically, we will use a novel contrastive loss function that measures the contextual similarity between the generated responses, and between the generated responses and the external context. This will allow us to identify which parts of the response are most likely to be hallucinations.
CONTROLS: We will compare our revised approach to the original counterfactual analysis method, and also perform an evaluation of the contextual similarity metric using a set of manually annotated datasets.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our revised approach may provide a more nuanced and accurate evaluation of hallucinations in retrieval-augmented generation, but it may require careful tuning of the contrastive loss function and may be sensitive to the choice of contextual similarity metric.

PROPOSAL: We will investigate whether hallucinations can be detected using a shared representation between the retrieval-augmented generation model and a pre-trained hallucination detection model. Specifically, we will fine-tune the pre-trained detection model on a set of labeled datasets and use the learned representations to predict hallucinations in a zero-shot setting.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed approach to existing transfer learning methods for hallucination detection, and also perform an analysis of the transferability of the learned representations across different model architectures and datasets.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our proposed approach may provide a more versatile and effective approach to hallucination detection, but it may require careful tuning of the pre-trained detection model and may not generalize well to all types of models and datasets.

PROPOSAL: We will develop a new theoretical framework for understanding hallucinations in retrieval-augmented generation, based on information-theoretic Principals. Specifically, we will establish a lower bound on the mutual information between the input prompt, the external context, and the generated response, and show that hallucinations can be detected by measuring the excess mutual information between the response and the internal knowledge.
CONTROLS: We will derive the theoretical bounds and assumptions, and compare our framework to existing approaches.
COST: 0 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our proposed framework may provide a fundamental understanding of the underlying causes of hallucinations, but it may require careful derivation and may not directly inform empirical hallucination detection methods.

PROPOSAL: We will incorporate hallucination detection into a multi-turn conversation between the user and the retrieval-augmented generation system. Specifically, we will train a dialogue manager to ask follow-up questions and receive clarification from the user in order to detect hallucinations and refine the generated response.
CONTROLS: We will compare our proposed approach to existing single-turn hallucination detection methods, and also perform an evaluation of the dialogue manager's ability to detect hallucinations and improve the accuracy of the generated responses.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Our proposed approach may provide a more effective and natural way to interact with retrieval-augmented generation systems, but it may require careful tuning of the dialogue manager and may not generalize well to all types of users and languages.

TITLE: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Masking-and-Reconstruction Tasks for Channel-Dependent Encoders in Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Experimentally compare the performance of two channel-dependent encoders, Residual Masking Convolutional Neural Networks (RM-CNNs) and Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks (TGCNs), on a set of real-world multivariate time-series forecasting benchmarks using the masking-and-reconstruction pretraining objective versus traditional supervised learning. We will train and evaluate the models on the Electricity Load Forecasting (ELF) dataset, a widely used benchmark in the domain of electricity consumption forecasting.
CONTROLS: Ideal Baseline: Unsupervised training of the two channel-dependent encoders; Frozen Baseline: Results from pretraining the encoders using masking-and-reconstruction tasks and then freezing their weights while training a simple linear decoder on the target forecasting task; Standard Baseline: A simple channel-independent encoder trained and evaluated using supervised learning.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect RM-CNNs to outperform TGCNs under the masking-and-reconstruction pretraining objective, particularly on tasks with short-term temporal dependencies, and that channel-dependent encoders will exhibit better forecasting performance compared to their channel-independent counterparts; however, improvements may be limited in tasks with highly variable or irregularly sampled temporal dynamics.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Different Decoder Architectures on Forecasting Performance in Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: Design and experiment with four simple, linear, and non-linear decoder architectures - Linear Projection, Fourier Transform-based Decoder, Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) Decoder, and Transformers-based Decoder - and evaluate their performance on a multivariate time-series forecasting benchmark using real-world weather forecasting data from the M4 Dataset. Specifically, we aim to analyze the performance difference between the proposed decoders, examine their sensitivity to the choice of encoder architecture, and investigate how incorporating stochasticity, such as dropout and Bayesian methods, affects forecasting accuracy.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Simple linear projection decoder; Frozen Baseline: A strong, pre-trained encoder paired with a fixed linear projection decoder.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the Transformers-based Decoder to yield state-of-the-art results, followed by the RNN Decoder and then Fourier Transform-based Decoder. Furthermore, we anticipate large differences in performance across the different decoders, suggesting that decoder architecture design is crucial in multivariate time-series forecasting.

TITLE: An Alternative to Masking-and-Reconstruction Tasks: Using Temporal Contrastive Learning for Pretraining Multivariate Time-Series Encoders

actions.texte:
ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Focal-Stack Guided Depth Estimation with Physics-Informed Neural Networks
PROPOSAL: Implement a physics-informed neural network (PINN) for DFF, where the network takes a focal stack as input and produces depth maps. The PINN will be trained to satisfy the physical principle of focus-sharpness relationship, incorporated into the network as a constraint: the network will predict the depth at which each pixel appears sharpest in the stack. The PINN will use the Adam optimizer, a mean squared error (MSE) loss function, and a subnet to predict the all-in-focus image from the input stack.
CONTROLS: Classical DFF methods, randomly perturbed PINN models, ablation study with and without the physics-informed constraint
COST: 1000 GPU-hours ( batch size = 16, mini-batch < focal stack size)
PREDICTION: The proposed PINN method will outperform classical DFF and learning-based DFF methods in benchmark performance, and provide more accurate and robust depth estimates, especially in areas with low texture, fine textures, or abrupt depth changes.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Focal-Stack Disentanglement for Robust DFF
PROPOSAL: Propose a technique to disentangle the spatial and focal dimensions of the focal stack, allowing for more robust DFF. This can be achieved by applying Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) to the input stack, to identify the latent variables that capture both the spatial structure and the focal evolution. Then, the network will be trained to predict the depth map from the disentangled latent factors, rather than the raw focal-stack images.
CONTROLS: Baselines with and without CCA, ablation study with different numbers of disentangled factors
COST: 500 GPU-hours (batch size = 16, mini-batch < focal stack size)
PREDICTION: The disentanglement technique will help the network better separate the texture-induced artifacts from true depth edges and gradient, and improve the robustness to fine textures, low-texture regions, and abrupt depth changes.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: REVISED Focal-Stack Disentanglement for Robust DFF
PROPOSAL: Instead of using Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) to disentangle the spatial and focal dimensions, propose a novel method using a variant of the Self-Modelling codes and Autoencoder (SMCAE) architecture, where the encoder will learn to separate the spatial features from the focal evolution, and the decoder will reconstruct the input stack from the learnt encodings. The spatial encoder and decoder will use a U-Net architecture for fine-grained feature extraction, while the focal encoder and decoder will use a simpler FCN to capture the focal evolution.
CONTROLS: Baselines with and without SMCAE, ablation study with different decoder architectures and complexity
COST: 800 GPU-hours (batch size = 16, mini-batch < focal stack size)
PREDICTION: The revised disentanglement method will improve the robustness to noise, texture-induced artifacts, and fine texture regions, and produce more accurate depth estimation compared to the original CCA method.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Focal-Stack Multimodal Loss for Ambient Occlusion Inference
PROPOSAL: Propose a novel focal-stack multimodal loss function that incorporates cues from both the spatial and focal dimensions to learn to infer ambient occlusion maps from the input stack. The loss function will combine a spatial part (e.g. PWC-Net based loss) with a focal part (e.g. a one-hot channel-wise squared distance between the predicted defocus map and the actual one). This will allow the network to learn to identify occluded areas that may be misclassified as sharp or faded due to geometrical ambiguities.
CONTROLS: Baselines using solely spatial loss, focal loss, and a combined spatial-focal loss
COST: 700 GPU-hours (batch size = 16, mini-batch < focal stack size)
PREDICTION: The multimodal loss will lead to improved ambient occlusion estimation, especially in areas with complex occlusion and focus mechanisms, and increase the accuracy in the final depth estimation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Optimizing Focal Stack Sampling with Reinforcement Learning
PROPOSAL: Use reinforcement learning to optimize the focal stack sampling strategy, given the goal to improve the depth estimation performance under a given focal stack sampling rate. The agent will explore different focal positions to maximize the performance. We will use Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm, which is efficient in finding the optimal policy for challenging tasks.
CONTROLS: Random sampling of focal stacks, other sampling strategies (e.g. uniform, grid-based), ablation study of learning rates and episode lengths
COST: 1500 GPU-hours (batch size = 16, maing multiple environment runs)
PREDICTION: By optimizing the sampling strategy, we expect a 10-20% increase in the depth estimation accuracy, especially in scenes with moving objects, reflectivity, or severe depth discontinuities.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Robustness of Focal-Stack Depth Estimation under Real-World Deformations
PROPOSAL: Evaluate how the proposed focal-stack depth estimation methods (FSPIN, Focal-Stack Disentanglement, and their combination) perform under real-world deformations, such as camera motion, scene deformation, and occlusion. The experiments will be conducted using a recently released dataset (Long-Room Charging Station or LM-Charging) specifically designed to mimic real-world environments. The performance will be evaluated on a simplified scenario of reposing the scene while maintaining the same set of objects and focusing on estimating scenes that achieve near identical setups but deviate slightly.
CONTROLS: Classical DFF methods, Focal-Stack Disentanglement, FSPIN without disentanglement
COST: 4000 GPU-hours (batch size = 16, full dataset processing)
PREDICTION: The robustness experiments will demonstrate that the combination of focal-stack disentanglement and physics-informed neural networks will exhibit resilience under various real-world deformations and a variety of conditions without compromising performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Focal-Stack Denoising Autoencoder for Low-Light Focal Stack Depth Estimation
PROPOSAL: Design a focal-stack denoising autoencoder to remove noise and artifacts from the input stack, improving the performance under low-light conditions. The autoencoder will be trained on synthetic low-light focal stacks and will be evaluated on real-world datasets with mixed lighting conditions. We will compare its performance with state-of-the-art methods and analyze its effect on final depth estimation.
CONTROLS: Original FSPIN models with and without the proposed denoising autoencoder, ablation study of the autoencoder architecture
COST: 1200 GPU-hours (batch size = 16, autoencoder training and evaluation)
PREDICTION: The proposed denoising autoencoder will significantly improve the depth estimation performance under low-light conditions, compared to the original FSPIN methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Uncertainty Estimation for Focal-Stack Depth Estimation with Density Networks
PROPOSAL: Implement density networks to estimate uncertainty for the proposed focal-stack depth estimation methods. The density network will be trained to predict a Gaussian distribution over the depths, allowing for uncertainty estimation and ensembling the predictions from different focal-stack depth estimation methods. This will enable evaluating the confidence of the predictions and improve the overall uncertainty estimation for real-world applications.

The PINN will be trained to satisfy the physical principle of focus-sharpness relationship, incorporated into the network as a constraint: the network will predict the depth at which each pixel appears sharpest in the stack. PROPOSAL 2: Focal-Stack Disentanglement for Robust DFF
Propose a technique to disentangle the spatial and focal dimensions of the focal stack, allowing for more robust DFF. This can be achieved by applying Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) to the input stack, to identify the latent variables that capture both the spatial structure and the focal evolution. PROPOSAL 3: Focal-Stack Multimodal Loss for Ambient Occlusion Inference

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Offline Robustified Quadrature Estimation (ORQE)
PROPOSAL: Introduce a new offline robustification method called Offline Robustified Quadrature Estimation (ORQE), building on the idea of robustified accumulation processes from our previous work. ORQE will leverage the quadric uncertainty ellipse to approximate the distribution of additive state offsets. We propose to estimate the ellipse parameters in an offline setting using a Generalized Gaussian Mixture Model (GGMM) adapted to the per-episode structure. The output of ORQE will be a confidence-quantified distribution of the removeable additive offset vectors for each episode. We then adapt the policy trained offline to utilize this distribution at test time.
CONTROLS: Compare against standard offline model-based and model-free baseline methods, and ablating the impact of GGMM when generating the confidence-quantified distribution.
COST: Estimated to require approximately 1,000 GPU hours (not including any downstream adaptation to actual models).
PREDICTION: We anticipate ORQE to outperform the baselines in a controlled simulation environment but may struggle with large drift episodes. With proper adaptation to specific domains, it may provide improved performance but may not deal with sparse datasets effectively.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Synthetic Dataset for Episodic Shift: RoboShift
PROPOSAL: Develop a synthetic dataset called RoboShift that models an episodic evolution of observation functions in a controlled robot navigation scenario, reflecting the real-world challenge mentioned in the problem statement. We will simulate the episodic offsets for multiple navigation tasks and provide with the scenario the past history of rendered navigation maps, ground truth of offsets, and possibly some renderings of real scenes.
CONTROLS: Examine the effect of gap size, gap distribution, and variability in per-dimension offsets on learning strategy of proposed methods trained on RoboShift (potentially also extending to similar environments).
COST: Estimated to require approximately 10,000 GPU hours for data generation and randomizing.
PREDICTION: We predict our ORQE method can generalize across multiple tasks within a single RoboShift dataset but predict an underfitting of unseen series since it would struggle when relying solely on GGMM (features used GGMM fit empirical extremes) and not incorporating a curt joined exploration-adaptation.

TITLE: Baseline Evaluation of GRPO for Agentic Search
PROPOSAL: Implement Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on a suite of real-world datasets for open-domain question answering and multi-hop question answering, to assess the baseline performance on these tasks. The experiment will use standard tools (e.g., zoo T5 model and PreTrained Knowledge Retriever) and evaluation metrics (e.g., accuracy, F1, and AUC-PR). We will also compare the baseline GRPO to a no-tuning/none approach and compare the relative baseline GRPO performance to state-of-the-art methods that use different optimization techniques.
CONTROLS: Baselines to be compared include a no-tuning T5 model with no down-stream fine-tuning, the same T5 with a simple prompt-based workflow for agentic search, and prior work that applied GRPO to these tasks.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: GRPO is expected to outperform the simple prompt-based workflow and have competitive performance with or better than prior work using GRPO, although GRPO may struggle with very complex or rare queries.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Intermediate Turn-Level Supervision through Group Consistency
PROPOSAL: Augment the GRPO objective with a group consistency term that encourages the model to produce diverse and informative intermediate turns within each rollout group. This is achieved by removing the penalty term that aligns rewards across groups when the number of unique intermediate actions across groups is zero. We will also encourage diversity by adding a entropy regularization term on the output of the model at each turn, so that the model cannot produce the same action multiple times in the same rollout. 
CONTROLS: This proposal will be compared to GRPO without group consistency term, and a model where the output of the model at each turn is discretized into tokens (to prevent overgeneration)  without entropy regularization.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect this method to improve upon the baseline GRPO by reducing advantage collapse, though the optimal amount of regularization for diversity will need to be determined. If too much regularization is added, the model may struggle to learn and converge slowly.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Intermediate Turn-Level Supervision through Group Consistency (Revised)
PROPOSAL: REVISED VERSION: In the previous proposal, we masked the penalty term for group consistency when the number of unique intermediate actions across groups is zero. However, this led to some unnecessary computation. A REVISED VERSION would subtract the maximum return of each rollout from the total group returns to ensure a clear distinction between rollouts is maintained but without additional overhead for computation. However, subtracting average rollout returns has shown success in providing a dense signal despite previous trials experiencing the problematic effect of zeroes in the denominator. 
CONTROLS: We also control for prior experiments using zero-adjusted returns but comparing performance between subtraction methods that have proven successful in theoretical environments but less in real.
COST: Same 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect this revised approach to provide good intermediate turn-level supervision signals that balance the competing goals of accurately modeling and improving subgroup diversity. If well-balanced, performance may actually exceed previous GRPO criteria, depending on how successful our methods are at pushing boundary.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Using a Hierarchical Rewards Structure
PROPOSAL: Design a hierarchical rewards structure where each turn receives a reward that is a weighted sum of two terms: 1) a task-relevant intermediate reward based on where each turn's intermediate action has influenced or forwarded progress toward achieving the ground truth final answer; and 2) a standard outcome-based reward term that has been normalized across all rollouts. The intermediate reward term encourages productive turn-by-turn behavior, while the normalized outcome term aligns progress toward producing the correct final answer. We will weight these two terms based on hyperparameters to find a sweet spot that balances intermediate supervision and outcome alignment.
CONTROLS: Experiment with a range of weighting hyperparameters to find the optimal mix of task-relevant and outcome-based supervision, using standard group relative policy optimization as a baseline.
COST: 180 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect this hierarchical rewards structure to improve performance in multi-turn search tasks by providing more focused supervision signals that distill the essence of each turn's contribution to the final result. However, precise tuning of the weighting parameters will be necessary to prevent the task from focusing too heavily on intermediate rewards at the expense of final task accuracy.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating a Knowledge Graph-based Debugging Tool for Agentic Search
PROPOSAL: Develop a knowledge graph-based tool to analyze and provide feedback on intermediate steps during the agentic search process. This tool can help identify areas where the model gets stuck or produces suboptimal intermediate results, reducing the information waste associated with outcome-only rewards. We will build a tool that leverages KG Query and stance scoring to predict task-relevant intermediate supervision signals based on the model's interaction history with the environment. Then we apply interaction weighting and cluster-reward comparison methods to broaden KG-exploration overlap significantly, as rewarded actions prove less positive according to ground truth final outcomes.
CONTROLS: Experiment using a KG-distribution predicited query-tool comparison and experiment against evaluation using the baseline system of hierarchical rewards alone as control
COST: 240 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This KG-based tool is expected to provide more informative feedback signals for intermediate steps and calibrate task-relevant productiveness, helping search agents cut down redundant later steps, although high annotations costs on some KG still is challenging.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Exploring the Limitations of Contrastive Learning for SPM Pre-training
PROPOSAL: Investigate the use of contrastive learning for pre-training Sparse Perception Models on unlabeled multi-view driving data, and analyze its limitations in capturing fine-grained 3D scene representations.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Train Sparse Perception Models from scratch on a labeled dataset (e.g., KITTI). Ablation: Use a different pre-training objective (e.g., masked autoencoders, NeRF-based approaches) to identify its impact on downstream task performance.
COST: Estimated compute in GPU-hours: 100
PREDICTION: We expect contrastive learning to improve pre-training performance over randomly initialized models but may not capture spatial-temporal geometry effectively, leading to limited performance gains on downstream tasks.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Evaluating the Effect of Temporal and Spatial Consistency on SPM Pre-training
PROPOSAL: Investigate the importance of temporal and spatial consistency in SPM pre-training by designing a framework that incorporates temporal and spatial constraints to encourage consistency in 3D scene representations across frames and in spatial arrangements of objects.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Train SPMs with existing contrastive learning objectives. Ablations: Remove temporal consistency (only spatial), remove spatial consistency (only temporal), remove both, to analyze their impact on downstream task performance.
COST: Estimated compute in GPU-hours: 150
PREDICTION: We expect that incorporating temporal and spatial consistency constraints will improve SPM pre-training performance, with the most significant gains coming from the combination of both, as this will capture both the dynamic nature of the scene and the spatial arrangement of objects.

ACTION: REVISE 
TITLE: Evaluating the Effect of Temporal and Spatial Consistency on SPM Pre-training
PROPOSAL: Revised Proposal: Modify the previous temporal and spatial consistency framework to incorporate a custom-defined similarity metric that measures the consistency of 3D scene representations across frames and in spatial arrangements of objects, using the GTF (Ground truth Fusion) algorithm to optimize the SPM's queries.
CONTROLS:  Baseline remains the same as the original proposal. 
COST: Estimated compute in GPU-hours: 300 (but taking the result of the baseline for half of this)
PREDICTION: We expect the revised framework, leveraging the optimized custom-defined similarity metric with GTF, to improve SPM pre-training performance more significantly, ensuring that the model captures both spatial and temporal consistencies effectively.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Transferring Scene-aware Queries for Efficient Domain Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Design a novel query-transfer mechanism that allows for the adaptation of scene-aware queries from a source domain (e.g., daytime driving) to a target domain (e.g., nighttime driving) without requiring fine-tuning or retraining the entire model, promoting efficient domain adaptation for various SPM-based applications.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Train SPMs from scratch on the target domain. Ablation: Use existing query-transfer methods (e.g., freezing a subset of layers) and compare with the proposed mechanism.
COST: Estimated compute in GPU-hours: 80
PREDICTION: We expect the proposed query-transfer mechanism to demonstrate robustness and efficiency in adapting to domain shifts while maintaining or even improving performance, addressing the limitations of existing methods in domain adaptation.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Pre-training SPMs on Unlabeled Data with Context-aware Bidirectional Temporal Transformers
PROPOSAL: Develop a pre-training framework that leverages bidirectional temporal transformers to capture complex temporal dependencies in unlabelled driving sequences, while incorporating context-aware encoder-decoder architectures to focus on relevant areas of the input frames, enabling more effective learning of 3D scene representations.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Train SPMs using existing contrastive learning objectives. Ablation: Remove the context-aware encoder-decoder, remove bidirectional temporal transformers to assess their individual contributions to pre-training performance.
COST: Estimated compute in GPU-hours: 220
PREDICTION: We expect the proposed pre-training framework to demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in capturing temporal dependencies and context-aware representations, with improved generalization to downstream tasks and reduced reliance on annotated data.

ACTION: REVISE 
TITLE: Pre-training SPMs on Unlabeled Data with Context-aware Bidirectional Temporal Transformers
PROPOSAL: Revised Proposal: Modify the context-aware encoder-decoder architecture to incorporate switches that select between BEV-centric and sparse query-centric representations based on the input data characteristics, enabling the pre-trained model to adapt to both dominant modalities and knowledge transferred to both BEV and query-based models.
CONTROLS: The baseline and ablations remain the same as the original proposal. 
COST: Estimated compute in GPU-hours: 280
PREDICTION: We expect the revised pre-training framework, leveraging the switches to adapt the context-aware encoder-decoder, to improve performance even more by captured spatial and temporal geometry in both dominant modalities effectively, transferring the knowledge to downstream tasks.

ACTION: REVISE 
TITLE: Pre-training SPMs on Unlabeled Data with Context-aware Bidirectional Temporal Transformers
PROPOSAL: Revised Proposal: Further modify the pre-training framework to incorporate a pruning mechanism that allows the model to allocate more capacity to learn salient features from the input data, by dynamically adjusting the number of context-aware switches and their corresponding complexity, adapting to the underlying data distribution.
CONTROLS: (same as the last revision's)
COST: Estimated compute in GPU-hours: 310
PREDICTION: We expect the revised framework, leveraging the pruning mechanism to allocate capacity dynamically, to improve learning efficiency in sparse regions of the input data, and further ensure the robustness of the pre-trained model in diverse environments.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Enhancing SPM Pre-training with Temporally-Aware Knowledge Distillation
PROPOSAL: Develop a pre-training framework that incorporates temporally-aware knowledge distillation to enable the model to leverage the temporal relationships between different frames and exploit the knowledge from a teacher model pre-trained on diverse sequences, improving the robustness and generalizability of SPMs to unseen scenarios.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Train SPMs using existing contrastive learning objectives. Ablation: Analyze the impact of different teacher models and Temporally-Aware Knowledge Distillation methods on pre-training performance.
COST: Estimated compute in GPU-hours: 180
PREDICTION: We expect the proposed framework to demonstrate improved generalizability and robustness by capturing temporal knowledge from diverse sequences, ultimately enhancing the overall performance of SPMs on naturalistic and real-world driving scenarios.

ACTION: REVISE 
TITLE: Transferring Scene-aware Queries for Efficient Domain Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Revised Proposal: Modify the query transfer mechanism to incorporate a domain-specific alignment module that allows for more effective adaptation of scene-aware queries from a source domain to a target domain, by jointly minimizing both the distance between the query sets and the similarity between their input representations.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Train SPMs from scratch on the target domain. Ablation: Analyze the impact of different domain-specific alignment methods on pre-training performance.
COST: Estimated compute in GPU-hours: 120
PREDICTION: We expect the revised query transfer mechanism, leveraging the domain-specific alignment module, to significantly improve adaptation performance and address the limitations of existing domain adaptation methods, ultimately enabling the rapid deployment of SPMs in new domains.

ACTION: ADD 
TITLE: Comprehensive Evaluation of SPM Pre-training using Real-World Benchmarks
PROPOSAL: Conduct a thorough evaluation of the proposed pre-training frameworks on a comprehensive set of real-world benchmarks, including KITTI, Cityscapes, and Waymo Open Dataset, to assess their performance in a naturalistic and diverse driving environment.
CONTROLS: Baseline: Train SPMs using existing pre-training objectives and evaluate them on the same benchmarks. Comparison: Evaluate the performance of each proposed framework on the selected benchmarks to assess their relative merits and limitations.
COST: Estimated compute in GPU-hours: 800
PREDICTION: We expect this comprehensive evaluation to serve as a thorough benchmarking and validation of the proposed pre-training frameworks, providing insights into their strengths and weaknesses, and ultimately contributing to the development of more effective and efficient SPM pre-training methods for real-world autonomous driving applications.

TITLE: Vision-Language Detector Test-Time Adaptation with Noisy Pseudo-Label Filtering
PROPOSAL: Experiment with biased-sampling semi-supervised learning on the target domain images with varying confidence thresholds for pseudo-label filtering and conduct an ablation study of how this affects detection performance on real-world benchmarks such as COCO and PASCAL VOC.
CONTROLS: Compare against self-training with pseudo-labeled objects and adapters activated only when necessary; use a pre-trained vision-language detector such as GLIP and its variants as the baseline; train and evaluate the detectors on standard object detection metrics such as AP and AP@IoU=0.5.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (using 4 NVIDIA V100 GPUs for 250 hours and 2 Tesla V100 for 250 hours).
PREDICTION: This approach might show initial improvements over existing self-training based methods but could also reveal degraded performance when confidence thresholds are high, due to the scarcity of pseudo-labels; however, adaptations could lead to lower performance than pre-trained detectors that haven't been adapted, especially in scenarios with abundant efficient target-domain data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Online Adaptation with Pretrained Feature Learning and Domain-Invariant Layer
PROPOSAL: Develop a TTAOD framework based on CLIP, which leverages domain-invariant layer (DIL) and a new adaptive learning mechanism that combines online learning from the unlabeled target images with self-training on pseudo-labels, while also leveraging the pre-trained feature learning capabilities of CLIP to reduce the need for finer-tuning.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the DIL and the proposed learning mechanism individually, in addition to the baseline CLIP model without any adaptation; compare against other existing adaptation methods using Faster R-CNN.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours (split into 5 phases of training and evaluation).
PREDICTION: This approach is likely to outperform pre-trained CLIP without adaptation due to the contributions from the DIL and online learning; however, may fail to surpass state-of-the-art TTAOD methods when confronted with vastly different target domains, or could also suffer from overfitting as the adaptation process would still be unsupervised.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Category-Agnostic Learning for Source-Free Test-Time Test-Time Adaptation
PROPOSAL: Design a novel adaptation framework that decouples category classification from object detection, allowing the model to learn an abstract representation of objects in the target domain regardless of category labels; use this representation to leverage knowledge distillation from a teacher network, and employ temporal ensemble methods during TTA.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance against category-aware adaptation methods and other TTAOD frameworks using metrics such as mAP and AP@IoU=0.75 on PASCAL VOC.
COST: 700 GPU-hours (trained on 3 NVIDIA A100 GPUs for 350 hours and 2 NVIDIA V100 for 350 hours).
PREDICTION: While category-agnostic learning can be beneficial in some open-world scenarios, it may complicate adaptation in domains where class categories remain consistent; on the contrary, this decoupling strategy could allow for adaptation to novel unseen categories present in target data, addressing one of the key limitations of standard TTAOD.

ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Revisiting Single-Step Image AR Sampling via Hierarchical Generators
PROPOSAL: We propose to explore single-step image autoregressive (AR) sampling using hierarchical generative models. Specifically, we will design a two-stage generative model, where the first stage outputs a coarse image representation and the second stage refines this representation. The key insight is that by dividing the image into coarse and fine-grained details, we can reduce the dimensionality of the autoregressive state space and therefore simplify the sequential sampling process. We will train the hierarchical generator using a combination of reconstruction loss and adversarial loss, and evaluate its performance on a range of image synthesis benchmarks.
CONTROLS: We will compare our hierarchical generator to the original AR model, as well as to existing one-step sampling approaches such as DD1. We will also investigate the effect of varying the number of stages in the hierarchical generator on its performance.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our hierarchical generator to outperform existing one-step sampling approaches, particularly on tasks that require high-quality image synthesis. However, we anticipate that its performance may degrade on tasks that require fast sampling, as the additional stages may increase computational overhead.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Efficient Single-Step Image AR Sampling via Localized Autoencoders
PROPOSAL: We propose to use localized autoencoders to reduce the dimensionality of the autoregressive state space and facilitate single-step sampling. Specifically, we will divide the image into a set of non-overlapping patches, and train an autoencoder to learn a low-dimensional representation for each patch. We will then use these representations to condition the autoregressive model, allowing it to generate each patch independently. By processing patches sequentially, we can achieve single-step sampling without sacrificing high-quality synthesis.
CONTROLS: We will evaluate our localized autoencoders on various image synthesis tasks, and compare their performance to the hierarchical generator and existing one-step sampling approaches. We will also investigate the effect of patch size and number on the performance of our method.
COST: 500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that our localized autoencoders will outperform existing approaches in terms of synthesis quality, particularly on tasks that require high-resolution images. However, their performance may degrade on tasks that require fast sampling, as the autoencoder training process can be computationally expensive.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Efficient Single-Step Image AR Sampling via Localized Autoencoders
PROPOSAL: We revise our localized autoencoders to use VQ-VAE (vector quantized variational autoencoder) instead of traditional autoencoders. Specifically, we will use a VQ-VAE to learn a discrete representation for each patch, which can be used to condition the autoregressive model. The discrete representation allows for efficient compression and decompression of the patch representations, making our method more computationally efficient.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our revised localized autoencoders to the original hierarchical generator, as well as to existing one-step sampling approaches.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (reduced due to the use of VQ-VAE)
PREDICTION: We expect our revised localized autoencoders to outperform existing approaches in terms of synthesis quality and computational efficiency. The use of VQ-VAE should significantly reduce the computational overhead, making our method more suitable for fast sampling tasks.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Improving Single-Step Image AR Sampling via Knowledge Distillation
PROPOSAL: We propose to improve single-step image AR sampling via knowledge distillation. Specifically, we will use the teacher-student distillation framework to transfer the knowledge from the teacher AR model to a student model, which can be trained to generate images in a single step. The student model will be designed to mimic the output distribution of the teacher model, while being computationally efficient.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our knowledge distillation method to existing one-step sampling approaches, including the hierarchical generator and localized autoencoders.
COST: 800 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our knowledge distillation method to achieve competitive synthesis quality with the state-of-the-art one-step sampling approaches, while being more computationally efficient. However, we anticipate that the knowledge distillation process can be sensitive to the choice of hyperparameters and teacher-student configurations.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Single-Step Image AR Sampling via Mixture of Experts
PROPOSAL: We propose to use a mixture of experts (MoE) framework to improve single-step image AR sampling. Specifically, we will design a MoE model that combines multiple expert networks, each of which generates a different portion of the image. The MoE model will be trained to decide which expert to use for each portion of the image, allowing for more flexible and adaptive sampling.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our MoE model to existing one-step sampling approaches, including the hierarchical generator, localized autoencoders, and knowledge distillation method.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our MoE model to achieve state-of-the-art synthesis quality and flexibility, particularly on tasks that require diverse and complex images. However, we anticipate that training and inference for the MoE model can be computationally expensive and challenging to optimize.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Efficient Single-Step Image AR Sampling via Localized Autoencoders
PROPOSAL: We revise our localized autoencoders to integrate a token alignment mechanism, which helps to align the generated tokens with the autoregressive model's prediction. This allows the localized autoencoders to better capture the dependencies between tokens and generate more coherent images. We will also investigate the effect of different token alignment strategies on the performance of our method.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our revised localized autoencoders to the original hierarchical generator, as well as to existing one-step sampling approaches, including knowledge distillation and MoE.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect our revised localized autoencoders to outperform existing approaches in terms of synthesis quality, particularly on tasks that require coherent and detailed images. The token alignment mechanism should help to improve the generated images' coherence and diversity, making our method more suitable for a wider range of applications.

TITLE: Exploring Faster Evaluation and Training Methods for Single-Step Image AR Sampling
PROPOSAL: We propose to explore faster evaluation and training methods for single-step image AR sampling. Specifically, we will investigate the use of parallel evaluation, mixed precision training, and gradient checkpointing to reduce the computational overhead of training and evaluating single-step AR models. We will evaluate the effectiveness of these methods on a range of image synthesis tasks and compare their performance to existing approaches.
CONTROLS: We will compare the performance of our faster evaluation and training methods to existing one-step sampling approaches, including the hierarchical generator, localized autoencoders, knowledge distillation method, and MoE.

However, we anticipate that the benefits of these methods may depend on the specific hardware and software environments used, and may not generalize to all image synthesis tasks.

PROPOSAL: We propose to augment single-step image AR sampling with uncertainty-aware inference. We will also investigate the effect of incorporating uncertainty-aware inference into the single-step AR sampling process on the quality and diversity of generated images.

TITLE: Jointly Adapting Optimization Components with a Shared Latent Space
PROPOSAL: Investigate an approach where all four optimization components (data augmentation, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function) are jointly adapted using a shared latent space, with each component being conditioned on the current state of the shared representation. This is achieved by combining a summarization network (e.g., Transformers) that aggregates the training dynamics into a compact latent vector, and a coordinator network (e.g., multi-task learning) that adjusts the components to conform to the latent representation. The shared latent space is learned end-to-end, and can capture complex interactions among the components.
CONTROLS: Compare to a baseline where each component is adapted independently, as well as an ablation study where only the coordinator network is included, and the summarization network is replaced with a static representation of the training state.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to yield improved performance by adapting the components to each other and to the evolving training state, particularly for tail classes. The shared latent space can introduce interactions between components, potentially leading to improved performance, but may also lead to overfitting if not regularized properly. 

Expected potential regimes of failure:
- When the summarization network is too broad and captures too much information, leading to overfitting on the training data.
- When the coordinator network is too weak and fails to effectively adjust the components.
- When the shared latent space fails to capture the relevant information from the training state, leading to suboptimal adaptation.

TITLE: Meta-Adaptive Optimization for Multi-Label Image Classification
PROPOSAL: Develop a meta-learning approach where a model learns to adapt its optimization components (data augmentation, optimizer, learning-rate schedule, and loss function) at multiple levels, each emerging from previous adaptations. This is achieved by iteratively injecting learned adaptations into the optimization process, such that each level builds upon the previous one. The model updates its parameters to maximize the performance of the previous adaptation, leading to a hierarchical structure of adaptations that can cope with the evolving training state.
CONTROLS: Compare to proposal (1), as well as a baseline where each adaptation is performed only once.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Expected to improve performance by fine-grained adaptation at multiple levels, particularly for tail classes. However, may become computationally expensive, and require careful design of the hierarchy to avoid overfitting.

While DPT+MoE should capture more diverse action distributions, we anticipate both to struggle on highly novel MDP structures not seen during training, due to the lack of fine-tuning to specific environments.
